title: Radio Hits
objective: After this level you can explain how radio created national hits.
summary: KDKA's 1920 broadcast began US commercial radio; by 1930, 40.3% of homes had a set and networks like NBC reached many cities at once. Payola showed airplay's value and led to a 1960 law.

cards.headline: In 1920, election night arrived through the air.
cards.body: On November 2, 1920, KDKA in Pittsburgh, recognized as America's first commercial radio station, went on the air with the Harding-Cox presidential election returns. What happens to music when a whole country can hear the same thing at the same moment?

cards.fact: In 1930, 40.3% of US households owned a radio: 12,048,762 homes.
cards.context: That count comes from the 1930 census, taken just ten years after KDKA's first broadcast. Put another way, roughly two homes in every five could now switch on a band without anyone leaving the living room.

cards.headline: One studio, twenty-one cities
cards.body: A single station only reaches so far. The fix was a network. NBC, the first organized national network, made its first broadcast on November 15, 1926, from New York over 25 stations in 21 cities, reaching as far west as Kansas City. Now one performance could land in living rooms across the country on the same night. That's the recipe for a national hit: everybody hearing the same song at once.

cards.headline: Airplay was worth a bribe
cards.body: If radio could make a song famous, getting on the air was worth money. Payola is an undercover payment to a disc jockey for promoting a record. In the payola scandal of the late 1950s, deejays took bribes to push certain records, and many lost their jobs. In 1960, largely because of those scandals, Congress amended the Communications Act, rewriting the rules on when broadcasts must say who paid for them.

cards.headline: Radio hits: tuned in
learned: 1930: 40.3% of US households owned a radio
Networks like NBC sent one show to many cities at once
Payola showed airplay was worth money; the law changed in 1960

questions.prompt: According to the 1930 census, about what share of US households owned a radio?

options.label: About 4 percent
options.rationale: Far more: over 12 million homes had one.

options.label: About 75 percent
options.rationale: That's too high for 1930; the census found 40.3%.

options.label: Nearly all of them
options.rationale: Roughly two homes in five had a set.

questions.explanation: The 1930 census counted 12,048,762 households with a radio: 40.3 percent.

questions.prompt: How did a network like NBC, launched in 1926, help create national hits?

options.label: It sent one program to stations in many cities at the same time
It sold records door to door in every state
options.rationale: NBC broadcast programs; it didn't sell records door to door.

options.label: It let listeners vote for songs by telephone
options.rationale: Its power was reach, not voting.

options.label: It replaced local stations with one giant transmitter
options.rationale: It linked many stations: 25 carried its first broadcast.

questions.explanation: Linking 25 stations in 21 cities meant one performance reached listeners across the country on the same night.

questions.prompt: From Level 29: what did airplay give a 1950s record that Petrucci's printing gave Josquin's masses?

options.label: Legal protection from being copied
options.rationale: Neither is about copyright; both are about reach.

options.label: A guaranteed payment for every performance
options.rationale: Payola paid deejays; airplay was valuable for its reach.

options.label: A reach to people the makers would never meet
Official approval from church or government
options.rationale: Neither was an official stamp; both spread music widely.

questions.explanation: Printed copies carried Josquin to choirs he would never meet, and radio could make a song famous, which is why airplay was worth a bribe.
